Can we treat them like the entertainment they are and tax them for the terrible ads?

hacker_news.title: Show HN: Agents infer Lego mechanisms from sources, then animate them
hacker_news.description: Hi there :) Around a month ago, I released LDraw Nova, an agentic toolset for assembling LEGO CAD models by generating LDraw source code files. For more details, here's the Show HN post: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49937916 From the comments, I got the impression that there was quite an interest in seeing not only AI-generated LEGO models, but also AI-animated LEGO ones. I took a look at results from past experiments, and found it feasible to use agentic LLMs for: - analyzing the LDraw source code for LEGO models - reverse-engineer! the mechanisms present by reading the descriptions and sequence for the parts there - and then, animate them via Blender! This new project I'm presenting, LDraw Mecha, is the end result and proof that can be done: - Read specially annotated LDraw LEGO models .mpd source files - Infer the model structure in terms of submodels - Select from those the ones that are mechanisms - Plan animations - Execute them in Blender In summary, from an initial .mpd source file, get a rigged and animated version for the model as a Blender (.blend) file. See the results here: - Repo (v0.5.0): https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/tree/v0.5.0 - Gallery: https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/GALLERY.m... - Process: https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/PROCESS.m... This project is very unusual, I'd really appreciate some feedback from the community. Cheers!

hacker_news.title: Show HN: Agentic Identity Broker, OAuth Delegation for AI Agents
hacker_news.description: Hi HN, I’m Jan. I am co-author of the Agentic Identity Broker (AIB), an MIT-licensed OAuth2 broker in the Zalando Incubator, that lets a user give an AI agent scoped, revocable access to MCP services. The broker solves three major challenges that are especially relevant in corporate environments: (A) Enable users to delegate workloads to agents without providing the agents all the user’s tokens. (B) Connect fragmented identity and authorization systems. (C) Centralize tool approvals and audit logging. We built AIB to fill an infrastructure gap in our own agent platform. At this moment in time, IETF working groups are still finalizing standards for agent identity, and vendors are still turning the necessary infrastructure into off-the-shelf products. We needed that infrastructure today. How it works: the user consents once per agent and service. The broker stores the third-party tokens encrypted. At request time a gateway (e.g. Agentgateway) does RFC 8693 token exchange. Agents never see user tokens and MCP servers only implement tools and don’t need to care about all the OAuth 2.1 plumbing. AIB is v0.1 and runs in production, bringing together hundreds of our agents with dozens of internal and external MCP servers. To try it locally: clone the repo, run "just compose-up-detached". The current features focus on on-behalf-of (OBO) use cases, where human actors delegate to agents. Next we are looking to also support headless agents, where agents are invoked by machines. Intent-based authorization is yet another package on our roadmap. If you’ve built either, or have feedback on the UI/UX, I’d like to hear from you!
